item.title: The Algorithm - the optimize trap
item.description:
Somewhere on your team there's a dashboard that's been rebuilt three times this year.

New filters. Better colors. A cleaner export button. Every version ships as a win.

Nobody has asked: does anyone actually act on what this tracks. If the answer is no, you've spent months polishing something that should have been deleted in week one.

The most common mistake a smart team makes is optimizing a thing that should not exist.

Comment SHINY if you've got a dashboard, report, or tracker like this right now.

The 5-step method that catches this before you polish it, free: github.com/SimonTheSalesBooster/the-algorithm

item.title: The Algorithm - automating the wrong thing
item.description:
Right now, someone on your team is building an AI agent.

It's wrapped around a workflow nobody has questioned in years. An approval chain. A report format. A hand-off between two people who don't even need to be in the loop anymore.

Nobody asked if the process should exist first. They just made it faster.

Ship it, and the same broken workflow just runs quicker. Now there's software holding it in place, and good luck ever pulling that back out.

Comment PAUSE if you or someone on your team is mid-build on an agent for a process that should have been deleted first.

The 5 steps to run before you build, free: github.com/SimonTheSalesBooster/the-algorithm

item.title: The Algorithm - the under-deletion tell
item.description:
Elon Musk's rule for cutting anything: if you never have to add back at least 10% of what you deleted, you weren't aggressive enough.

Most people cut the easy 20%. The safe stuff. The stuff nobody would miss anyway. Then they stop, call it done, and never touch the parts that were actually load-bearing.

Real cutting means occasionally guessing wrong. You delete something, someone screams, you put it back. That's proof the knife was sharp enough.

Comment SAFE if you've cut processes before and never once had to bring anything back. That usually means the cuts were never that aggressive to begin with.

Musk's full 5-step method, free: github.com/SimonTheSalesBooster/the-algorithm

item.title: The Algorithm - the unowned requirement
item.description:
There's a meeting on your calendar right now that nobody remembers requesting.

An approval step. A recurring report. A weekly sync that has run for two years straight.

Ask five people why it exists and you get five different guesses. Ask who owns the requirement, the actual name of a person who could kill it, and the room goes quiet.

That silence is the tell. No named owner means it survives by default, not by merit.

Comment OWNER if you've got one of these running right now and you genuinely don't know whose call it was.

The 5-step method that catches these before they multiply, free: github.com/SimonTheSalesBooster/the-algorithm

item.title: AI agents on broken processes
item.description:
Everyone is racing to build an AI agent this month.
Almost nobody is asking if the process underneath it should exist at all.
An agent bolted onto a bloated workflow doesn't fix the workflow. It runs the bloat faster, and now there's software wrapped around it that's much harder to ever pull back out.
Before you build the agent: question every step, delete what nobody can name an owner for, simplify what's left. Then speed it up. Automate last, not first.
That order is the whole difference between an agent that removes work and one that just industrializes a mess.
Free skill, five steps, no infrastructure required to try it: github.com/SimonTheSalesBooster/the-algorithm

item.title: Sales processes need a knife
item.description:
Most sales processes don't need a new tool. They need a knife.
Extra approval on the SOW. A CRM field nobody fills in. A forecast call that exists because it always has. Every one of those got added by someone, at some point, for a reason that made sense that week.
Nobody ever goes back and asks if it's still earning its place. That's how a 4-step sale quietly turns into a 9-step slog nobody can explain.
The 8 Steps of the Repeatable Sale we teach every client used to be twice as long. We questioned every stage, cut the ones that made the seller feel busy instead of moving the buyer forward, and only then built anything to speed it up.
Fewer moving parts isn't the compromise. It's the whole method.
Before you add another approval or another field, question it first: github.com/SimonTheSalesBooster/the-algorithm

item.title: The approval step nobody owns
item.description:
A team asked me: "can we add an approval step before this goes out, and build a dashboard to track how long approvals take?"
Ran it through The Algorithm instead.
Question: who owns the requirement that this needs approval? No name, no reason. Just a leftover from when the team was three people.
Delete: remove the approval step. Replace it with a standard the sender checks themselves.
Simplify: one checklist, three items.
Accelerate: sends go out same day now, not whenever the reviewer opens their calendar.
Automate: nothing yet. Not until the manual version runs clean for a month.
No dashboard needed. The thing it measured should not have existed.
github.com/SimonTheSalesBooster/the-algorithm

item.title: Delete before you automate
item.description:
Delete before you automate.
Elon Musk drills this into every engineering team at SpaceX, Tesla, and Boring Company (it's in Isaacson's biography). Five steps, always in this order:
1. Question every requirement. No named owner, delete it. 2. Delete the part or process. If you're not adding back 10%, you weren't aggressive enough. 3. Simplify what survives. 4. Speed it up. 5. Automate. Dead last, always.
Skip to step 5 first and you just spent real money automating a mistake, faster.
We turned it into a free Claude Code skill.
Free. Open-source. Grab it: github.com/SimonTheSalesBooster/the-algorithm

item.title: 8 Steps Repeatable Sale - DM funnel
item.description:
Every deal that's gone right for the 2,400 people we've coached followed the same 8 steps, in the same order.
Every deal that's stalled skipped one.
Step 4, for one: "What happens if you do nothing?" Most people skip straight past it and wonder why the deal goes quiet.
Skip a step and the deal stalls. Run them in order and the close feels obvious. Most people are still guessing which step they skip.
I've never published the one-pager we run internally. Still has the coffee-ring stains from a hundred real calls. All 8 steps, in order.
DM me READY and I'll send it over.

item.title: Sales isn't the goal
item.description:
Sales is not something to strive for.
It is what happens after you help someone make real progress on a problem they are stuck on.
Can I help you solve this. Can we build this together. Can we break through that wall. That is the fun part, and it is the only part that earns you the right to ask for the close.
Chase the close first and buyers feel it. Chase the problem first and the close finds you.
Clip from my conversation on Doing Business with a Servant's Heart with Steve Ramona.

item.title: Dinner with Jesus and Schnitzel
item.description:
Steve Ramona asked me a question I was not ready for: reserve a table in Vienna, invite three people who shaped your life, then pick the meal.
Schnitzel, obviously, we are in Vienna. The harder part was the guest list. I left seats open on purpose. The people who show up uninvited are usually the ones worth having there.
Some questions are not about tactics. They are about who belongs at the table once the tactics stop mattering.
Full conversation on Doing Business with a Servant's Heart with Steve Ramona, link in comments.

item.title: The nicest people close the fewest deals
item.description:
The nicest people on sales calls close the fewest deals.
After 23 years coaching sales conversations, that is the pattern I keep seeing. They listen. They say yes to everything the buyer asks for. The buyer leaves calling them a great resource.
Then nothing happens.
Service does not mean surrendering control. It means preparing so well that you can lead the conversation toward a decision, not give away an hour of free consulting.
The people who actually help buyers are the ones running the call, not agreeing with it.
Clip from my conversation on Doing Business with a Servant's Heart with Steve Ramona. Full episode link in comments.

item.title: I fired my CRM
item.description:
Five months ago I stopped opening a CRM.
Not because I stopped tracking pipeline. Because I do not have to click through one anymore.
I ask one question: who are the three people I need to follow up with today. My AI agent checks every conversation, finds what I promised, drafts the exact offer I owe, and drops it in my Gmail draft folder. I just say send.
It coded its own CRM inside Notion in ten minutes. I cancelled Salesforce the same week.
43 agents running my pipeline. 200 dollars a month. That is the entire stack now.
If you are still logging activity by hand, you are not behind on AI. You are behind on delegation.
Clip from my conversation on Doing Business with a Servant's Heart with Steve Ramona. Full episode link in comments.

item.title: Tailwind Tuesday repo launch
item.description:
Most shoutout posts online get scrolled past. The author picks whoever they met yesterday and the reader can feel the lack of substance.
Here is what we have been doing instead.
Every Tuesday at 8am Vienna, an agent we built scans the past 28 days of my calendar, my call transcripts, and my coffee bookings. It picks ONE human I have had at least three real touchpoints with that month. Then it checks: have I actually witnessed a superpower, an act of integrity, or a moment of loyalty from this person? If the answer is yes with concrete evidence, it drafts a 5-line shoutout. If the answer is vague, it skips the week.
The post celebrates THAT person. Their LinkedIn. Their work. Their ICP.
Zero CTA back to me. No mention of my offers. No "DM me to learn more." The whole thing is a gift, or it does not ship.
We call it Tailwind Tuesday 🪂
The world has too many promoters and not enough endorsers. So we built the system, ran it for a while, and today we open-sourced it.
Take it. Fork it. Build your own version for your own network. The README has the full architecture, the agent prompt, and a sample post showing what passes the evidence test (and what fails).
If three of you build your own Tailwind Tuesday this month, the experiment was worth it.
→ github.com/SimonTheSalesBooster/tailwind-tuesday
PS .. yes, the post you might be reading from me one of these Tuesdays could be about you. The agent does not know yet who it picks next week. Neither do I.

item.title: Jetpack Sheet — what it is
item.description:
Most founders watched an AI workshop last quarter. How many have an agent running today? Almost none.
The gap is not the content. It's the install step.
We just shipped the Jetpack Workshop Execution Sheet.
Six rungs from "I watched the workshop" to "my first agent in production":
1. Pick the one trigger you want automated 2. Write the 5-question agent brief 3. Test it in a sandbox thread 4. Install it on your machine with screenshots and troubleshooting 5. Connect the one tool that matters 6. Run it for 72 hours, log what breaks, iterate
Step 4 is where most guides die. We wrote it with the same screenshots we use inside the paid Jetpack cohort.
This is the ladder most founders are missing.
Link in comments.

item.title: Sales forces shrinking (evergreen)
item.description:
Block cut 40% of its workforce. Stock jumped 18% the same day.
The sales floor as we knew it is over.
Recent shifts: .. Block: 10,000 to 6,000 employees. Profit guidance raised +54%. .. Salesforce: 9,000 to 5,000 support roles. Benioff on record: "I need less heads." .. Meta: $2.4M revenue per employee. Up 85% in 3 years. .. 36% of B2B companies cut their SDR team. Highest cut rate of any role.
The pattern is identical everywhere. Headcount down 30 to 50%. Revenue per employee up 15 to 85%. Markets rewarding every announcement.
The quiet version is scarier. Most companies aren't firing reps. They just stopped backfilling when reps leave.
If you run a B2B business with 5 to 10 people, the question isn't "will this reach me?" It's "which of my 3 competitors rebuilds their GTM first?"
Move first. Own the advantage.
Grab a coffee if this is where you are: calendly.com/simonseverino/coffee-with-simon
